worker_notes: Identity independently verified: title The Dark Versus Bright Side of a Smiley: A Preregistered Replication of Experiment 3 in Glikson et al. (2018) “The Dark Side of a Smiley”, Linda Lai and Lewend Mayiwar, Collabra: Psychology 9(1), 2023, DOI 10.1525/collabra.90195, printed p. 1. This is a primary empirical replication report with Methods, Results, discussion, references and appendix, not an abstract-only parse or preregistration. The supplied text spans 13 printed pages. No PDF supplied; embedded figure contents are not recoverable from this text and were not visually inspected. The neutral description does not distinguish warmth versus competence, main effects versus formality interactions versus mediation, or gender-controlled versus uncontrolled specifications. Page 5 contains multiple tests and page 9 contains conclusion prose. No row correspondence can be established from the descriptions and page locators. Targets were not assigned by audit_id order or numeric matching. Input replication locator p. 5. UNASSIGNED printed candidates (Cohen’s d; same-test p bounds preserved): gender controlled, p. 4 warmth smiley main effect d=0.47, p<.001, F(1, 818)=44.64; warmth interaction d=0.11, p=.108, F(1, 818)=2.58. Without gender control, p. 5 warmth main effect d=0.48, p<.001, F(1, 843)=47.77; warmth interaction d=0.09, p=.169, F(1, 843)=1.89. Gender controlled, p. 5 competence smiley main effect d=0.22, p=.002, F(1, 818)=9.67; competence interaction d=0.12, p=.090, F(1, 818)=2.88. Without gender control, p. 5 competence main effect d=0.20, p=.003, F(1, 843)=8.81; competence interaction d=0.09, p=.197, F(1, 843)=1.67. Moderated mediation p. 6: warmth index=-0.05, 95% CI=-0.12, 0.005; competence index=-0.12, 95% CI=-0.25, 0.01; numeric p not supplied in that section. These indices are not d. Authors explain d conversion from partial eta-squared on pp. 4 and 8; no conversion performed here. Table 4 p. 8 also contains formality main effects and appropriateness effects, further precluding unique correspondence. These candidates are neither a target assignment nor an exhaustive list of every test in the paper. Candidate participant analytic N=823 explicitly given for gender-controlled analyses; final sample N=847 for analyses without gender control. Speed and nondifferentiated responding exclusions apply to final sample; main analyses do not exclude manipulation-check failures. Gender-controlled analyses additionally exclude 24 participants not reporting male or female. Candidate Ns are printed, not inferred from df. No arithmetic or N summation performed. Neither N assigned to unresolved row. Reported success is the authors’ overall verdict on the key interaction findings under their small-telescopes assessment, not a row-specific verdict or an assertion that all component effects failed. Unassigned original-side fields are placeholders only.

coding_context.description: Due to perceptions of (in)appropriateness, the use of smileys may backfire and produce less favorable perceptions of competence in a formal work-related setting, yet more favorable perceptions of warmth in an informal work-related setting.
coding_context.reported_success_quote: The authors of the original study reported support for their proposition that [...] the use of smileys may backfire and produce less favorable perceptions of competence in a formal work-related setting, yet more favorable perceptions of warmth in an informal work-related setting.  Our results, in contrast, indicated that smileys produce a negative effect on perceptions of competence and a positive effect on perceptions of warmth, regardless of the level of formality.
